title: Team Members Over-Interpret the Actions of a New Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note describes how team members, anxious about a new leader's arrival, obsessively over-analyze small and seemingly insignificant actions -- meeting order, workspace choices, even where the leader parks -- searching for clues about future priorities. Rather than dismissing this as irrational, the piece argues leaders should harness it deliberately, since team members will draw inferences from their choices whether intended or not. The practical recommendation is to be intentional about sequencing and salience -- putting the most important people, issues, and meetings first on purpose during the crucial early period.
points: New leaders are subject to intense, often irrational scrutiny as team members search for clues about priorities.
Small choices -- meeting order, workspace setup, even parking -- get over-interpreted as signals of intent.
Rather than dismiss this behavior, leaders are advised to harness it by acting intentionally during onboarding.
Sequencing the most important people and issues first is recommended so inferences match true priorities.
This over-interpretation is described as most intense during the 'honeymoon phase' of a new leadership role.
quotes: team members engage in an active hunt for meaning in everything the new leader does.
In the search for meaning and certainty, team members make big inferences from the small acts and choices a new leader makes.
Since leaders can’t prevent team members from drawing conclusions about their often random choices, they have the opportunity to become more intentional about what they do.
Whatever is most important (initiatives, people, customers, issues) should come first on purpose.
Team members have a need to predict how the leader will engage in the future and will continually draw inferences from nearly all actions and choices during the honeymoon phase.
